lines.text: Goosebumps are your body trying to puff up fur you don't have anymore.
Every hair on your skin has a tiny muscle attached to it.
When you're cold or scared, those muscles pull the hairs upright.
For furry animals, that's useful. Raised fur traps air and keeps them warm.
It also makes them look bigger. Think of a frightened cat, or a porcupine raising its quills.
We lost most of our fur, but kept the reflex.
Scientists call it a vestigial reflex, a leftover from our ancestors.
That's why you can still get chills from music, or a scary movie.
Your body is still trying to look bigger, with fur that's barely there.

sources.claim: Arrector pili muscles pull hairs upright; considered a vestigial reflex; in furred animals it insulates and makes them look larger (cats, porcupines); triggered by cold, fear, awe and music

publish.title: Goosebumps Are Leftover Fur 🐈
publish.description: Why your skin gets bumpy when you're cold, scared, or listening to a great song. It's a reflex from our furry ancestors.
